template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a stateless Palestinian. I was born in the United Arab Emirates, where I lived with my family until I was 18 years old. I completed my high school studies there. Because the cost of higher education was too high in the UAE, I left in 2010 to study in Jordan. I lived in Jordan for seven years, from 2010 to 2017, under a study permit. During my time in Jordan, I completed my studies and tried to find employment, both in my field and in other areas. However, I was unable to secure any job because I am a Palestinian. Employers in Jordan would not hire me due to my status and the travel documents I hold. As a Palestinian, I do not have permanent residency in Jordan and cannot work legally there. After my studies ended in 2018, I searched for employment in Jordan, the UAE, and Lebanon, but I was not hired in any of these places because of my Palestinian status and the type of travel documents I possess.

In 2017, I traveled from Jordan to Lebanon to apply for a Canadian student visa and to obtain my identity documents. While I was in Lebanon, a terrorist group attempted to recruit me. I was able to obtain my Canadian visa and left Lebanon for Canada in 2017. I have Lebanese travel documents issued to Palestinian nationals, but these do not allow me to return to the UAE. I am not permitted to enter the UAE with these documents, and I do not know the specific reason for this restriction. If I were to attempt to return to the UAE as a non-resident without proper documents, I would be detained in very harsh conditions. I fear that I would face cruel and unusual punishment due to the detention conditions there. I cannot return to Jordan because, as a Palestinian, I am denied the right to work and live a decent life. I am unable to return to any of these countries because of my stateless status and the risks I face.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 27-year-old Sinhalese from the capital of my home country. After spending two years in London, U.K., I returned home in 2006 and became involved in politics. I worked for a political party during the municipal elections under the guidance of a family friend, who is a well-known politician. I was an active member and served as a special assistant to this politician. During the election campaign, the Election Commission rejected our party’s candidature because one candidate was not 18 years old by the nomination deadline. As a result, our party allied with another party, which eventually won the municipal elections.

During and after the elections, I received death threats from the opposition party and, in particular, from the supporters of a powerful politician. The situation escalated in mid-2006 when I witnessed the mayor being bribed by a criminal working for the opposition. The criminal tried to convince the mayor to break our party’s alliance and form a new one with the opposition. I ran away and immediately informed my political mentor about what I had seen. The two men involved in the bribery noticed my presence and, according to what I was told, wanted to eliminate me. I was warned that if they ever saw me again, they would kill me.

After this, I went into hiding. Thugs associated with the powerful politician came to my home and beat up my uncle and other family members while searching for me. Fearing for my life, I left my home country on October 5th, 2006, and arrived in Toronto the same day. I claimed refugee status 13 days later.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a minor and lived in my home country with my mother, father, and sibling. In 1998, my parents used all their savings to build a house on land that the government had leased to them. In 2001, the government decided to expropriate the land for a road-widening project and ordered us to remove our house. This was happening to other families in our area as well. My father and several others organized a protest against the expropriation and the lack of fair compensation. As a result, my father and four others were arrested, convicted, and sentenced to three years in jail.

After my father was imprisoned, the government demolished our house. My sibling and I were suspended from school because of our father's political activities and his imprisonment. We were not allowed to return to school while we remained in our home country. The authorities made it clear that our suspension was a direct consequence of our father's actions and his status as a political prisoner. This situation caused us to lose access to education, which is essential for our development and future. We did not know if or when we would be allowed to return to school, as our ability to do so depended on whether our father would be released from prison, which was uncertain.

Because of these events, I fear that if I return to my home country, I will continue to be denied an education and face serious harm due to my relationship to my father, who is considered a political activist by the authorities.

I have been attacked by such groups on several occasions and am afraid to return because of them. I left Hungary and came to Canada to escape these threats to my safety and life. Before coming to Canada, I was on medication for depression and anxiety, including tranquillizers, due to the trauma I experienced. My name is {FULL_NAME}. In late 1994, I bought an apartment unit where I lived with my daughter. In mid-2011, the city government issued a notice to all residents of our apartment complex, telling us we had to vacate the building by the end of the year. The compensation offered by the government was unfair, so I, along with other residents, organized a protest to push the authorities to negotiate a better deal. Although the authorities met with our representatives and promised to look into the matter, we were still required to leave by the deadline.

On a day in 2011, I joined other residents in a demonstration in front of the government building. During the protest, a security guard pushed me and I fell. Some residents retaliated, and the situation escalated. Reinforcements arrived, the demonstration became violent, and two residents were badly hurt. I saw two police officers coming toward me, so I ran away and went into hiding.

While I was in hiding, I learned from my aunt that the Public Security Bureau (PSB) came to my home looking for me, accusing me of organizing people to protest against the government. They threatened that if I continued to hide, they would go after my family. I also learned that three other protesters were arrested. Later, my building was demolished, but the PSB continued to visit my aunt’s home and other relatives’ homes looking for me to arrest me.

Arrangements were made through a smuggler for me and my daughter to obtain US visas and fake Hong Kong passports. The smuggler accompanied us from my home country to Canada via the United States. Since arriving in Canada, I have been told that the PSB continues to visit my relatives’ homes looking for me. I left my home country in 2011, arrived in the United States the same day, and then traveled to Canada, where I applied for refugee status.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a Tamil male from my home country, born in the Jaffna District. I lived most of my life in two towns in that region and was self-employed. In 2006, my brother and his family were abducted by an armed group, and to this day, their whereabouts are unknown. That same year, I fled to another area due to shelling but returned to my hometown in 2007. There was a camp of the same armed group about 200 yards from my house. I was taken there and interrogated. Members of this group regularly harassed me, tried to force me to join them, and extorted money from me. In 2008, they extorted 20 lakhs from me and threatened to turn me over to the army, accusing me of supporting another armed group. I fled the north and traveled to the capital that same month.

On a day in 2009, I was arrested by the police with 10 other Tamil males. I was questioned and badly beaten by a police officer, then detained for seven days. The night I was released, I was abducted by unknown persons, beaten in a white van, and detained in a room for almost one month. My kidnappers demanded a ransom of 15 lakhs from my parents for my release. My parents paid the ransom, and I was released from detention.

After my release, I was able to leave my home country in 2009 and fled to Thailand. From there, I boarded a ship called the Ocean Lady and arrived in Canada on October 17, 2009. I fear returning to my home country because I have been targeted by armed groups for extortion and forced recruitment, and I have been accused of supporting an opposition group. I am also afraid that the authorities in my home country would know or quickly learn that I traveled on the Ocean Lady, a ship suspected of carrying members of the opposition group, and that I would be subject to detention, torture, or even death upon return. I fear being interrogated about my connections, my journey, and the people I traveled with, and I am at risk throughout the country, with no protection from the authorities.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a citizen of my home country and I am of mixed ethnicity: my father is an ethnic Hungarian and my mother is Roma, specifically Romungro. Because of my parents’ mixed marriage, I am perceived as Roma in my community. Throughout my life in my village, my family and I experienced daily harassment due to our ethnicity. People on the street would spit on us, insult us, and threaten us with racist remarks. Swastikas were drawn on my parents’ graves. In 2010, while I was with my daughter, people started calling us names. When I spoke back, I was assaulted and received bruises.

I completed grade eight and then four years of vocational education, graduating in 1989. I worked in a store for about a year, but I was let go when my employers found out I was Roma. My children also faced discrimination. They were denied proper education and were insulted and threatened at school. My daughter was beaten many times and had to go to the hospital as a result. My husband, who was a dark-skinned Roma, was also harassed. In 1995, he died in suspicious circumstances. The police concluded it was a suicide, but he was likely murdered by nationalists or racists, as there was no reason for him to take his life and the circumstances were suspicious.

After my husband’s death, I went back to school and obtained two certificates, but I was unable to find work and had to rely on public assistance. I did not go to the police for help with the harassment and threats because I did not believe they would help, given their record and the nature of the issues. The discrimination and mistreatment my family and I experienced were ongoing and affected every aspect of our lives, including education, employment, and daily activities. In 2011, I borrowed money and relocated to Canada. I cannot return to my home country because the risk of discrimination and mistreatment extends throughout the country, and even the capital would not be a safe place for me.

I was sentenced to 120 days of house arrest, a fine, and three years probation. The court allowed me to use cannabis during my sentence, but the prosecutor appealed, and my conviction for possession of mescaline was reinstated as a felony. I sought to serve my sentence in San Francisco, where attitudes toward medical cannabis are more tolerant, but ultimately, I left the United States for Canada before serving my sentence, while the details of my sentence were still being resolved. My family had already moved to Canada for business reasons. I did not return to the United States to serve my sentence, and a warrant was issued for my arrest. When I returned, I was questioned by officials at the Passport Office. After that, I started receiving threatening phone calls that insulted my Jewish background. In 1997, I was attacked and beaten by members of a nationalist group and needed hospitalization. My wife was also attacked. We reported these incidents to the police, but they did not help us.

In 1998, I was attacked again by uniformed members of the same group. They forced me into their patrol car and took me to the central police station, where I was detained for 48 hours. During this time, I was interrogated three times and physically and verbally abused. When I was released, I was told to pick up my passport from the District Police near my home. When I went there, the police officer insulted me with anti-Semitic slurs before returning my passport.

Afterwards, I received more threatening calls at work from nationalist groups. My car was vandalized and anti-Semitic graffiti was painted on it. The police refused to investigate and shifted me to another section. When I met with the head of the District Police, he recorded my statement but warned me not to speak against the nationalist group. In 1998, my son was attacked and hospitalized, but the police did not take it seriously.

I began making arrangements to leave my home country. I tried to move to Israel and also prepared documents for immigration to Canada. Threatening calls and vandalism continued. In the summer of 1998, I was attacked and beaten again, and the police warned me not to speak out. After another attack in the fall of 1998, I reported my problems to the City Administration, but nothing happened. In 1999, after another brutal beating, I was able to get a visa for myself and left for Canada in July 1999. I was persecuted because of my Jewish ethnicity, could not get protection from the authorities, and I fear for my life if I return.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. My family has a long history as hereditary Chiefs of a tribe in the region where I grew up in my home country. About fifty years ago, my great uncle, concerned that he might not have male descendants, temporarily transferred the Chieftaincy to his brother-in-law. However, the brother-in-law kept the Chieftaincy within his own family, and since then, our two families have been in conflict over who is the legitimate Chief. My father considers himself the rightful Chief and has tried for years to regain the Chieftaincy, but has not succeeded.

Around 1980, a descendant of the brother-in-law assumed the Chieftaincy. I served as secretary to the Town Development Committee during the 1980s and early 1990s. The Chief came under criticism for selling land and not accounting for the proceeds. I acted as the main accuser and, at a public meeting in 1991, demanded that the Chief explain his actions. At that meeting, the Chief threatened to kill me. Initially, I thought it was an empty threat, but three days later, a relative of the Chief warned me that the threat was real. This warning, along with an offer of a teaching position in another town, led me to move away. There, I met and married my wife and raised my children.

During my absence, three people filled in for me at the committee. In 2003, the first died suddenly. In 2004, the second went blind while meeting with the Chief, and later that month, the third became ill with a mysterious disease. These events were caused by the Chief using magic. In 2005, after hearing that my father was seriously ill, I returned with my family to our hometown. I resumed my position with the committee and, together with others, scolded the Chief for trying to get free cement for his personal use. The Chief threatened me again. In 2006, I lodged a complaint against the Chief with the committee and the Council of Elders, who rebuked him. Shortly after, four of the Chief’s nephews confronted and beat me. Friends intervened and chased them away. My maternal uncles reported the incident to the Chief, who blamed me for the beating. One uncle approached the police, but they dismissed the complaint. Members of the committee feared for my safety and urged me to attend a conference in Canada. Once in Canada, I sought protection.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a thirty-five year-old citizen of my home country. Between 2000 and 2002, I worked as a photographer for a daily newspaper in my hometown. In the summer of 2000, I took photographs of a man who died under suspicious circumstances in a court building. The newspaper published these photographs. After this, the editor of the paper and I were required to report to the Ministry of Guidance, where we were reprimanded. The authorities then prohibited me from taking photographs in certain areas.

In 2002, I took video and still pictures of New Year celebrations in a part of my hometown. The police arrived to break up the celebrations and detained me along with others. While in custody, the authorities mistreated me and kept me in jail for eight months. When I was released, it was on conditions, and I was required to report to the authorities on several occasions.

After my release, I returned to work with my former editor, who had started a new publication because the authorities had closed the previous newspaper. I became involved in taking photographs at special events at the local university, where I got to know students who opposed the government. Through these contacts, I assisted the students in getting materials printed and helped them distribute those materials at various demonstrations.

In 2003, these students held large public rallies, and I attended some of them. The authorities raided the university and arrested some students who had worked with me. A week later, the police stopped and detained my brother while he was driving my car. They held him for a week and told him they were looking for me because I had participated in demonstrations and helped the student protesters. I became concerned for my safety, believing the authorities may have identified me through photographs taken at the demonstrations or from information given by the arrested students. I went into hiding. With the assistance of one of my brothers and an agent, I left my home country and came to Canada. I fear that if I return, the authorities will detain, torture, and possibly kill me.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I completed my legal studies in 1997 and began my career as a deputy public prosecutor in 1999. In 2007, I was appointed to the position of justice of the peace court. I joined the magistrates’ union in 2003 and became the steward for my office, later being elected as general treasurer of the union’s executive committee in 2007. As a member of the bargaining committee, I worked with government representatives to implement an agreement following a union strike in 2011.

On the day the agreement was to be implemented, I was summoned to the police special services office. When I arrived, I was arrested without formal charges and detained for a week. During my detention, I was questioned about my affiliation with opposition parties, especially because I belonged to the same tribe as a prominent opposition figure. I was also rebuked for my union involvement and accused of seeking to undermine the president’s image ahead of the presidential election.

After my release, the union committee continued its activities cautiously. In 2013, the magistrates’ group became impatient with the slow implementation of the agreement and decided to hold a surprise 48-hour work stoppage. I was responsible for notifying union members by sending text messages. Shortly after, an order was issued against me, and I was detained for 10 days, accused of inciting magistrates to protest against the government.

Following my release, I was transferred to another peace court. There, I was assigned a case involving a political opponent. The authorities expected a heavy sentence, but I dismissed the charges against the political opponent, going against the government’s wishes. As a result, I received threats by telephone and was abducted outside my union office. I managed to escape from captivity when my jailers were distracted.

Fearing further arbitrary arrest, I decided to leave my home country for the United States while my visa was still valid. After arriving, I suffered a serious accident that delayed my journey to Canada, where I eventually claimed refugee protection. I am perceived as being affiliated with the opposition after refusing to collaborate with the regime to convict a political opponent, and I continue to fear persecution if I return.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 27-year-old man from my home country. I have lived my entire life there, but I have always had to hide my sexual orientation. My family does not know that I am gay, and I have never been able to live openly because of the attitudes in my society and the conservative environment in which I grew up. I fear returning to my home country because of my sexual orientation. In my country, being gay is considered a crime, and the law allows for up to one year in prison for what is described as sexual intercourse against nature. Even though this law is not always enforced, it is still in effect, and it creates a climate of fear and discrimination for people like me.

Members of the LGBT community in my country face both official and societal discrimination. If someone is outed, they are likely to lose their job and face abuse from the police. There have been incidents where the police have arrested people suspected of being gay, subjected them to humiliating procedures, and even forced them to undergo physical exams to determine their sexual orientation. The authorities have supported these actions publicly. Because of this environment, I was always in the closet and could not live as myself.

I came to Canada in 2012, and for the first time, I was able to live openly as a gay man. I do not want to return to my home country because I would have to hide who I am again or face serious risks if I tried to meet other gay men. If I returned, I would have to live a life of celibacy or constant fear for my safety. There is no place in my country, not even the capital, where I could live safely as an openly gay man. The police are agents of harm, and I would not be able to seek protection from them. Instead, there is a strong likelihood that I would be victimized by the police because of my sexual orientation. This is why I am seeking protection and do not want to return.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a woman from my home country who suffers from a serious mental illness, specifically bipolar disorder with psychotic features. Over the years, my illness has required me to be hospitalized in several countries, including Lebanon, my home country, the United States, and Canada. My first major mental health crisis occurred when I was working in Lebanon in 1997-98, which led to a fifteen-day hospital stay. After returning to my home country, I continued to struggle with my mental health. I was treated by a psychiatrist at a hospital in the capital, and I was admitted as an in-patient under his supervision. He prescribed me anti-depression medication, and I found him to be caring and helpful.

However, after my discharge, I faced strong negative attitudes from my relatives and friends. They pressured me to stop taking my medication, telling me it was damaging my brain, and they also persuaded me to stop seeing my psychiatrist. Without my medication and treatment, my condition worsened, and I became unstable again. The stigma surrounding mental illness in my home country is very strong. People often associate any form of mental illness with madness, and it is common for those with mental health issues to be ostracized or even restrained at home until their symptoms subside. Hospitalization is seen as a last resort, and there is little understanding or support for people like me.

My family situation is also difficult. My mother is raising my young son in the United States, and my sister is planning to emigrate there as well. I have only one other relative in my home country, my father, but I have been estranged from him for a long time. I fear that if I return, I will not have any meaningful family or community support. As a woman with a mental illness, I am particularly vulnerable. In my home country, the burden of care for mentally ill family members falls disproportionately on female caregivers, and women with mental illness face even greater discrimination and isolation.

I am afraid that if I return to my home country, I will be pressured again to stop my treatment and medication, which would put my health and safety at serious risk. Without support, I could end up homeless or worse. The stigma and lack of understanding about mental illness, combined with the absence of family support, make it dangerous for me to return.
